title: Make a sprite sheet from your pixel-art frames
description: Create trimmed sprite atlases with padding, edge extrusion, and animation metadata. PixelWall Pro costs $15 once; drawing and native saves are free.
intro: Draw and organize frames in the editor, then export a packed, horizontal, vertical, or grid atlas. Pro includes a PNG atlas with JSON metadata and a game package ZIP. Choose trimming, padding, and edge extrusion for your game pipeline.

steps.title: Create your frames
steps.text: Choose New project in the header, enter Width and Height, and draw a pose. Use + Frame, Duplicate, or Duplicate linked in the timeline.

steps.title: Define a clip
steps.text: Select frames in the timeline. Open Edit clips, choose Create clip from selected frames, and set its Name, Direction, and Repeats (0 loops continuously). Duration ms edits selected frames.

steps.title: Set the export
steps.text: Open Export. Choose Sprite atlas PNG or Game package ZIP, set Scale and Clip, then choose Layout, padding, extrude, Trim transparent edges, and Power-of-two dimensions.

steps.title: Keep the metadata
steps.text: Sprite atlas PNG creates image and JSON downloads. Allow both downloads and keep them together. Game package ZIP keeps its atlas, JSON, rendered frames, editable project, and any tilemap assets in one archive.

sections.heading: Trimming and playback
paragraphs: Trimming removes transparent borders and records each frame’s original size and offset in JSON. Edge extrusion repeats border pixels outside the frame rectangle; padding separates entries. Packed layout does not rotate sprites.

The editor exports the selected clip’s playback sequence, including reverse and ping-pong order. The default Clip choice uses the active clip when one exists. Choose a clip containing all required frames when you want the complete animation. Atlas JSON includes source IDs and durations; it is not the classic editor’s older Phaser-specific animation recipe schema.

sections.heading: What is included
paragraphs: Drawing, animation editing, scripting and the command API are free. Editable PixelWall and supported sprite files, plus individual PNG, BMP and TGA frame exports, are free. Pro is $15 USD once for animated GIFs, sprite sheets and atlases, game package ZIPs, and saved export presets.

The document engine accepts canvas sides from 1 to 65,535 pixels, with at most 4,194,304 canvas pixels, up to 256 layers including groups, and up to 2048 frames. A document may store at most 16,777,216 image pixels across its distinct images. Linked cels share image data. Browser canvas limits and available memory can be lower, especially for very wide sprites. Check representative artwork on your device.

links.label: Read the current export format reference
Automate sheets and atlases with the CLI

faqs.question: Can I make a sprite sheet without an account?
faqs.answer: Yes. Drawing, frames, layers, scripts, and project files are free without an account. Sprite sheet and atlas downloads require Pro, a $15 one-time purchase.

faqs.question: Does the PNG include animation timing?
faqs.answer: The pixels do not. Keep the accompanying JSON, which records frame rectangles and durations. The game ZIP keeps metadata and images together.

faqs.question: Can I use the older Phaser or PixiJS examples?
faqs.answer: Yes. Those existing guides identify the classic export workflow at /editor/classic. Its animation recipe schema differs from the current atlas JSON.

title: Animate pixel art one frame at a time
description: Animate pixel art with onion skin, named clips, and frame timing. Draw and preview free; export animated GIFs with PixelWall Pro for $15 once.
intro: Build animation with editable layers, per-frame timing, and named clips. Duplicate a pose, use onion skin to compare neighboring frames, and preview forward, reverse, or ping-pong playback. Editing is free; Pro adds GIF and atlas exports.

steps.title: Draw a pose
steps.text: Create a project and draw on the active image layer. The timeline is always below the canvas.

steps.title: Add frames
steps.text: Use + Frame for a blank frame or Duplicate for an independent copy. Duplicate linked reuses the same cel image; edits to linked copies affect the shared pixels until you choose Unlink selected cels.

steps.title: Use onion skin
steps.text: Open the Effects panel. Set Previous onion frames, Next onion frames, and Onion opacity to compare neighboring poses. Onion overlays do not appear in exports.

steps.title: Set timing and clips
steps.text: Select frames using Shift for a range or Command/Ctrl for individual selection. Adjust Duration ms. Open Edit clips to create a clip from selected frames, name it, and choose Direction and Repeats (0 loops continuously).

steps.title: Preview and export
steps.text: Press Play animation or Space. Open Export, choose Animated GIF, then set Scale and Clip. Save an editable project backup as well.

sections.heading: Procedural 2D motion
paragraphs: Effects → Motion and particles opens controls for baked position animation and deterministic particles on selected frames. The results are editable cels. Keep separate frames or an undo point before applying a bake.
These are ordinary 2D drawing operations. PixelWall does not generate artwork with embedded AI, and it does not currently provide a 3D model rendering workflow.

sections.heading: Timing, color, and capacity
paragraphs: The current GIF encoder reserves a transparent entry and keeps up to 255 distinct opaque colors per frame. More colorful frames are quantized to a 216-color RGB grid. Alpha below 128 becomes transparent; other pixels become opaque.

GIF delays round to 10 ms units with a 10 ms minimum in the current encoder. Some viewers impose a longer minimum. The editor limits the complete scaled GIF sequence to 67,108,864 output pixels; choose a smaller scale or shorter clip when needed.

The document engine accepts canvas sides from 1 to 65,535 pixels, with at most 4,194,304 canvas pixels, up to 256 layers including groups, and up to 2048 frames. A document may store at most 16,777,216 image pixels across its distinct images. Linked cels share image data. Browser canvas limits and available memory can be lower, especially for very wide sprites. Check representative artwork on your device.

faqs.question: Is animation editing free?
faqs.answer: Yes. Frames, timing, clips, linked cels, onion skin, playback, and 2D motion editing are free. Pro unlocks the listed batch and animation exports.

faqs.question: Does a linked duplicate make a separate drawing?
faqs.answer: It shares the cel image. Use an ordinary Duplicate or Unlink selected cels when the pixels must diverge.

faqs.question: Do imported GIFs keep layers?
faqs.answer: No. A GIF contains rendered frames, palette colors, transparency, and timing. It does not carry your original editable layer structure.

title: Trace a reference with the classic pixel-art projector
description: Use the classic PixelWall reference projector to align a photo or sketch, then draw pixels on separate layers. Reference tracing and PNG saves are free.
intro: The adjustable photo and sketch projector is in the classic editor. Open it below to position a reference behind a square pixel canvas, then trace by hand. The current editor also supports reference layers, with a different layer-based workflow.

sections.heading: Open the matching editor
paragraphs: The steps on this page describe the classic Reference panel, Image Scale, Move Image, and Add Trace Frame controls. They are available at /editor/classic. Use a separate project backup when moving between classic projects and the current v4 editor.

In the current editor, choose Reference or Layers → Import reference layer. Adjust its layer opacity and cel offsets. Reference layers remain visible in the editor preview and stay in editable projects. Rendered exports omit them by default; enable Include reference layers when you deliberately want them in the output.

steps.title: Choose your grid
steps.text: Use New Project to create a blank canvas, such as 16 × 16 or 32 × 32. Keep a backup of existing work when prompted.

steps.title: Load a reference
steps.text: Open Reference → Load Image and choose an image from your device.

steps.title: Line it up
steps.text: Adjust Opacity and Image Scale. Use Move Image to position the reference, then finish adjusting. For a pixel reference, Match 1:1 Pixels aligns one source pixel with one canvas cell.

steps.title: Draw your version
steps.text: Select Pencil and a color, then trace the shapes you want. Use Eraser, Fill, and additional Layers as needed. Add Trace Frame creates another blank frame over the same reference.

steps.title: Save your work
steps.text: Choose Export → Current Frame for a PNG of your artwork. Use Save Project for an editable backup that also includes the reference.

sections.heading: What is included
paragraphs: Reference loading, positioning, tracing, layers, PNG downloads, and project backups are free. Choose from square canvases of 8, 16, 24, 32, 48, 64, 96, 128, or 256 pixels per side. The reference stays on your device and is excluded from exported artwork, but it is included in your saved .pixelwall project.

faqs.question: Does PixelWall automatically convert a photo into pixel art?
faqs.answer: No. The image is a drawing reference. You choose the colors and place the pixels yourself. Supported sprite strips can also be imported directly as editable frames.

faqs.question: Will the reference show up in my PNG?
faqs.answer: No. Artwork exports include your visible drawing layers, not the projected reference. A saved .pixelwall project includes the reference so you can continue tracing later.

faqs.question: Can I trace one sprite at a time from a sheet?
faqs.answer: Yes, when PixelWall detects a supported horizontal or vertical strip of square sprites. Choose Use … Grid if offered, then use Previous sprite and Next sprite to align each reference with the canvas. Use Add Trace Frame when you need another blank drawing frame.

title: Draw your tiles and build a map with them
description: Draw pixel-art tiles, check repeating seams, and paint a tilemap in your browser. Tiled-compatible map packages are included in PixelWall Pro.
intro: Create independent tilesets from selected frames, then paint reusable tiles on tilemap layers. Tiles can be flipped or rotated in quarter turns. Keep the editable map and source tiles together in a .pixelwall project or a Pro game package.

steps.title: Draw source tiles
steps.text: Use one canvas-sized tile per frame. Select the frames to include in your tileset.

steps.title: Create the tileset
steps.text: Open Tiles, choose Create tileset from frames…, and confirm Create from selected frames. The tileset stores independent image records; later changes to the source animation frames do not automatically redraw those tile records.

steps.title: Make room for the map
steps.text: If needed, resize the canvas after creating the tileset so multiple tiles fit. Canvas resizing changes the document bounds; tiles retain their own dimensions.

steps.title: Paint a tilemap layer
steps.text: In Tiles, choose the tileset and Add tilemap layer. Select a tile, then draw on the canvas. Use Erase tile, Flip horizontally, Flip vertically, and Rotation for cell edits.

steps.title: Inspect and export
steps.text: Use Seamless preview to inspect repetition of the rendered frame. Save the native project. With Pro, choose Export → Game package ZIP to include independent tilesets and Tiled-compatible map files.

sections.heading: Edit a reused tile
paragraphs: Choose Tiles → Edit tile pixels…, then click a painted tilemap cell. Edit the original tile pixels in the small canvas; the cell keeps its rotation and flip settings.

Tile edit mode controls reuse: Auto reuses a matching tile or adds a new one; Manual updates every use of the tile; Stack always adds a new tile. Choose Apply tile pixels to commit the change. Source animation frames remain independent from the copied tileset.

sections.heading: What the package preserves
paragraphs: The game ZIP includes manifest.json, sprites.png, sprites.json, rendered frame PNGs, and the editable project. Projects with tilemap data also include maps/ files and tilesets/ files. Tiled maps group layers by tile dimensions for each animation frame.

The export carries tile IDs, quarter-turn and flip flags, layer opacity, visibility, names, and source metadata. Its manifest reports unsupported Tiled blend modes. Collision objects and animated-tile definitions are not generated; the rendered frame PNGs and native project retain the full artwork.

sections.heading: Classic Tilemap Lab
paragraphs: The older frame-as-tile Tilemap Lab remains in the classic editor, including its original one-map export workflow. It is distinct from independent tilesets and tilemap layers in the current editor.

links.label: Open the current Tiled package guide

sections.heading: Capacity
paragraphs: Drawing, animation editing, scripting and the command API are free. Editable PixelWall and supported sprite files, plus individual PNG, BMP and TGA frame exports, are free. Pro is $15 USD once for animated GIFs, sprite sheets and atlases, game package ZIPs, and saved export presets.

The document engine accepts canvas sides from 1 to 65,535 pixels, with at most 4,194,304 canvas pixels, up to 256 layers including groups, and up to 2048 frames. A document may store at most 16,777,216 image pixels across its distinct images. Linked cels share image data. Browser canvas limits and available memory can be lower, especially for very wide sprites. Check representative artwork on your device.
A tilemap layer can contain up to 1,048,576 cells, with no more than 2048 rows or columns. Browser memory can become a practical limit earlier.

faqs.question: Will editing a source frame update every tile?
faqs.answer: Current-editor tilesets are independent copies created from frames. To change a reused tile, choose Edit tile pixels…, click a tilemap cell, and use Manual to update every use or Auto/Stack to keep an independent variant. The classic Tilemap Lab has a separate frame-linked workflow.

faqs.question: Does PixelWall export Tiled maps?
faqs.answer: Pro Game package ZIP exports Tiled-compatible orthogonal maps and external image-collection tilesets when the document contains tilemap layers. Keep the archive folder structure intact.

faqs.question: Can I import a Tiled map back into PixelWall?
faqs.answer: Direct Tiled map round-trip import is not currently offered. Keep the .pixelwall source project.

title: Build Willowmere: an end-to-end pixel-art world
description: Build the revised Willowmere world in PixelWall: animated scenery, editable characters, reproducible CLI commands, a versioned viewer, and a marketing gallery.
intro: Follow Willowmere, The Lantern River, from a small riverbank to two animated environments and expressive characters. The art direction edition adds richer scenery, turning waterwheels, and an editable character composition, with a complete versioned viewer and reproducible downloads.

sections.heading: The finished world
paragraphs: Willowmere is a woodland route held together by a winding river, warm lanterns, and a shared 32-color palette. The top-down valley and side-view Lantern Ford use the same visual language. Mira, the river courier, and the mosslight reedling bring that setting down to character scale.

This project used an external AI coding agent to author supported PixelWall commands and pixel buffers, followed by visual review and revisions. PixelWall supplied the editable layers, cels, palettes, timeline, and rendered exports. PixelWall contains no AI model, and no externally generated image was imported as artwork.

Updated art direction edition: the environments now have fuller tree crowns, richer paths and masonry, revised water accents, and twelve-phase turning waterwheels. A separate Lantern Ford composition puts both characters on editable PixelWall paint layers. The viewer loads one complete asset release before showing the artwork or starting playback.

media.caption: Willowmere overworld. The editable source is 512 × 384 pixels; this preview is enlarged for viewing.

Lantern Ford: 768 × 256 pixels, 13 layers, 12 frames at 100 ms per frame.
Lantern Ford showcase: 768 × 256 pixels, 20 layers, 12 frames, with the characters retained on independently editable layers.
Mira: 32 × 48 pixels, three painted layers, 20 poses across Idle, Walk, and Jump.
Mosslight reedling: 40 × 32 pixels, three painted layers, 14 poses across Idle and Walk.

sections.heading: 1. Open the files and set up the CLI
paragraphs: For an immediate look, download the native projects below and choose Open project or image in PixelWall. Inspect the layers and named animation clips, then save an independent copy before experimenting. The original workflow was tested with desktop 0.5.0; the downloads page supplies the current release.

To reproduce the artwork, extract the public package into a new working folder. Install Node.js 22.13 or newer, download the official CLI ZIP, and extract its contents into tools/cli inside that folder. The CLI bundle includes its dependencies; no npm install is needed. Run every command below from the extracted package root. Use a folder with enough free disk space for the generated projects and PNGs.
sections.code:
node --version
node tools/cli/pixelwall.mjs help
node tools/cli/pixelwall.mjs inspect projects/overworld.pixelwall
mkdir -p reproduced
node tools/cli/pixelwall.mjs render projects/sideview.pixelwall --frame 11 --scale 2 --out reproduced/ford-preview.png

links.label: Download the editable Lantern Ford character composition

sections.heading: 2. Start with a tiny animated riverbank
paragraphs: The starter exercise is a 128 × 96 RGBA scene. It teaches the same construction method as the larger world: broad shapes for the ground and river, named layers for separate visual roles, linked cels for static artwork, and a few deliberately animated details.

Create a blank project, apply the saved command batch once, then run the small Lua detail. The finished document should contain nine named layers and twelve 100 ms frames. Open it and play the Riverbank • 1.2s clip. The banks and roots stay fixed, the crown moves gently, and pale streaks travel across the teal water.
sections.code:
mkdir -p reproduced/tutorial
node tools/cli/pixelwall.mjs new --width 128 --height 96 --name Riverbank --out reproduced/tutorial/empty.pixelwall
node tools/cli/pixelwall.mjs apply reproduced/tutorial/empty.pixelwall --commands tutorial/riverbank-commands.json --out reproduced/tutorial/riverbank.pixelwall
node tools/cli/pixelwall.mjs script reproduced/tutorial/riverbank.pixelwall --script tutorial/reeds.lua --timeout 10000 --out reproduced/tutorial/finished.pixelwall
node tools/cli/pixelwall.mjs render reproduced/tutorial/finished.pixelwall --frame 11 --scale 4 --out reproduced/tutorial/frame11.png

media.alt: A small pixel-art riverbank with teal water, pale ripples, a mossy tree, grasses, and a reed clump.
media.caption: The starter exercise uses a 128 × 96 canvas and a twelve-frame timeline.

links.label: Read the starter exercise and expected result

sections.heading: 3. Use Lua for a small detail
paragraphs: The reeds.lua script draws a detached 16 × 16 reed clump and attaches it to all twelve frames. It does not loop over the whole canvas or use file or network access. Broad rectangles, polygons, ellipses, and lines are a better fit for large areas; small pixel loops are useful for a tightly bounded detail.

A cel holds a layer’s image at a particular frame. Adding a detail only to frame zero will make it disappear later unless you deliberately expose or link it across the timeline. An early version of this exercise missed an exposure; the final supplied exercise corrects it and was rebuilt independently.

Try a small revision: in tutorial/riverbank-build.mjs, change Math.round(Math.sin(f*Math.PI/6)) to Math.round(2*Math.sin(f*Math.PI/6)). Run node tutorial/riverbank-build.mjs to regenerate the commands, then repeat the lesson into a new output folder. Compare the original one-pixel sway with the windier two-pixel version.

links.label: Learn bounded editing and operation recovery

sections.heading: 4. Compose the world before adding detail

steps.title: Give the scene a readable route
steps.text: Use the river and paths to guide the eye between the mill, bridge, waterfall, ruin, orchard, village, and landing. Establish those large shapes before decorating the banks.

steps.title: Assign colors a job
steps.text: Deep blue-green defines outlines and shadow, teal separates water from land, cream and pale green pick out foam and light, and coral and brass give the characters and lanterns warm accents. The saved 32-color palette travels with the projects.

steps.title: Separate structure from motion
steps.text: Keep buildings, banks, trunks, and the bridge anchored. Put ripples and tree crowns on layers that can change without moving their surroundings. Link unchanged cels instead of repainting every frame.

steps.title: Review at native size
steps.text: Check the route, focal points, and silhouettes at 1×, then enlarge with nearest-neighbor scaling to inspect pixel edges. Add texture only where it improves readability.

media.alt: A wide side-view pixel-art landscape with a lantern-lit mill, wooden bridge, water, mossy banks, and distant trees.
media.caption: Lantern Ford uses a 768 × 256 canvas. The environment is a layered pixel-art scene; gameplay is added separately.

sections.heading: 5. Rebuild the two environments
paragraphs: This edition starts from the earlier environment projects included in base/. The exact final edit manifests rebuild the revised scenery and animation on those projects. Use the earlier public package, linked below, to study the initial blockout, completion, detail, and polish stages from a blank canvas.

The helper applies at most 100 commands and approximately 8 MB per batch. Run the sequence into fresh output files so the supplied originals remain intact. Each successful batch commits independently; a failed batch does not roll back earlier completed batches.

The final command composes the unchanged courier and reedling pixels onto the revised side view with supported PixelWall cel commands. It adds contact shadows and separate painted character layers. The resulting marketing composition is a native editable project.
sections.code:
mkdir -p reproduced
node source/apply-bounded.mjs base/overworld.pixelwall source/overworld-final.json reproduced/overworld.pixelwall
node source/apply-bounded.mjs base/sideview.pixelwall source/sideview-final.json reproduced/sideview.pixelwall
node source/apply-bounded.mjs reproduced/sideview.pixelwall source/showcase-final.json reproduced/lantern-ford-showcase.pixelwall
node tools/cli/pixelwall.mjs inspect reproduced/lantern-ford-showcase.pixelwall
node tools/cli/pixelwall.mjs render reproduced/overworld.pixelwall --frame 11 --out reproduced/overworld-11.png
node tools/cli/pixelwall.mjs render reproduced/sideview.pixelwall --frame 11 --out reproduced/sideview-11.png

sections.heading: 6. Redesign characters around clear silhouettes
paragraphs: The first small character drafts did not read clearly enough. The revision enlarged the canvases and rebuilt the poses around recognizable faces, accessories, and weight. This was an art-direction choice, not a PixelWall size limit.

Mira has a stepped hood, visible face, coral scarf, stitched satchel, brass lantern, and distinct airborne poses. The reedling has a curling teal tail, moss mantle, and antler lantern. Both projects separate the artwork into Body • silhouette and weight; Cloth, leather & lantern; and Face & small highlights.

The three layers contain painted pixels you can edit independently. Try changing a scarf or lantern accent while leaving the body silhouette untouched, then check every pose for consistent placement. The character manifests are already generated and included. Build from a new empty project when replaying them.
sections.code:
mkdir -p reproduced/characters
node tools/cli/pixelwall.mjs new --width 32 --height 48 --name Mira --out reproduced/characters/courier-empty.pixelwall
node source/apply-bounded.mjs reproduced/characters/courier-empty.pixelwall source/character/courier-v2.json reproduced/characters/courier.pixelwall
node tools/cli/pixelwall.mjs render reproduced/characters/courier.pixelwall --frame 16 --scale 4 --out reproduced/characters/mira-jump.png
node tools/cli/pixelwall.mjs new --width 40 --height 32 --name Reedling --out reproduced/characters/reedling-empty.pixelwall
node source/apply-bounded.mjs reproduced/characters/reedling-empty.pixelwall source/character/reedling-v2.json reproduced/characters/reedling.pixelwall

media.alt: Comparison of the earlier small courier sprite and the larger redesigned Mira with a readable hood, face, scarf, satchel, and lantern.
media.caption: The character revision prioritized silhouette, facial readability, and distinct animation poses.

sections.heading: 7. Give each motion its own clip
paragraphs: The environment loops use twelve 100 ms frames, or 1.2 seconds. This edition adds a twelve-phase turning waterwheel to each scene alongside changing water highlights and restrained canopy motion. Static roots, banks, and architecture remain linked and anchored.

The frame numbers below are zero-based, matching the CLI. In a timeline that displays frames starting at 1, add one. Idle poses last 180 ms; walk and jump poses last 100 ms. Use the named clips to preview each action rather than treating the complete pose collection as one continuous movement.
items: Mira: Idle 0–5, Walk 6–13, Jump 14–19. Idle and Walk loop; Jump is a one-shot clip.
Reedling: Idle 0–5 and Walk 6–13. Both clips loop.
Check silhouettes at native size, foot placement, transparent margins, and the transition from the last loop frame back to the first. Different frame data alone does not prove that motion feels good.

media.alt: Fourteen mosslight reedling poses showing its curling tail, moss mantle, lantern antlers, and idle and walk motion.
media.caption: The reedling’s fourteen poses, shown together to compare silhouette and movement.

sections.heading: 8. Continue in the desktop editor with an agent
paragraphs: Desktop MCP was BLOCKED in this revision’s test: read-only inspection timed out, and PixelWall displayed ECONNRESET and EPIPE connection errors. Their cause remains unresolved. This edition used the CLI for creation, rendering, and native checkpoints; no new desktop edit, library save, artifact checkpoint, or cross-interface reopen is claimed. The connection instructions below remain an optional workflow reference.

The CLI rebuild works without a running editor. For live desktop editing, open PixelWall, enable Help → Allow local agent connection, and choose an approved export folder. Configure your agent with the official pixelwall-mcp.mjs launcher from the CLI bundle, following the desktop MCP guide. The connection controls the opted-in local window; it is not a hosted service.

Have the agent inspect the current project and revision before applying a bounded edit. Use expectedRevision so an intervening human edit cannot silently be overwritten. For long operations, retain the operation ID and poll until completion; staged progress is not a committed edit.

After visual review, export a native project checkpoint under a new filename. Ask the desktop artifact tool to save it to the approved folder, verify the delivered file, then inspect and render it with the CLI. Editing, library saving, export generation, and a verified disk checkpoint are separate outcomes.

sections.heading: 9. Export frames and build a viewer
paragraphs: Keep the native .pixelwall files as the editable source of truth. Individual frame PNGs retain transparency and are enough to reproduce the viewer. The command below exports all twenty Mira poses to a new folder; use ranges 0,13 for the reedling and 0,11 for either environment.

GIF, sprite-sheet, atlas, and game-package generation require Pro. Updated desktop Pro GIF/sheet export was BLOCKED in this revision, so the revised environments are supplied as individual PNGs and externally encoded MP4 loops. The earlier edition’s desktop Pro exports are historical assets; they are not presented as revised exports. The character projects remain unchanged.

The public viewer loads PixelWall PNG exports. Its JavaScript supplies keyboard movement, jumping, camera follow, parallax, and a 24-second tour. These are viewer features, not PixelWall gameplay or collision tools. The download includes the viewer source and frames so you can inspect that boundary or build your own presentation. It is a demonstration, not a finished game.

A preview delivery issue in the local handoff mixed older and newer artwork after files were replaced at the same URLs. The published revision uses a separate immutable release folder, preloads every environment frame, near layer, parallax background, and character frame, and waits for all images to decode. A failed load keeps playback stopped and offers a retry. Older release assets remain available at their original URLs.

node tools/cli/pixelwall.mjs export projects/courier.pixelwall --format png --frame-range 0,19 --out-dir reproduced/mira-frames
node tools/cli/pixelwall.mjs inspect projects/courier.pixelwall

sections.heading: 10. Verify the handoff and keep the failures visible
paragraphs: Independent CLI review reopened all three revised scene projects and compared all 36 rendered frames as decoded RGBA pixels: 12 overworld, 12 side-view, and 12 Lantern Ford showcase frames. All matched. The twelve side-view parallax layer composites also match their corresponding full scene before camera transforms. The two character projects are unchanged from the previous edition.

The original desktop library-save failure remains FAIL. Large imports were previously BLOCKED by the same library budget. This revision’s desktop MCP connection was also BLOCKED, so the newer CLI checks must not be read as a successful revised desktop save or cross-interface test. Native file delivery preserves editable artwork independently of those failed or blocked operations.

The supplied final manifests replay onto the included earlier environment projects. Use the public validation summary for this edition’s reproduction checks. Keep input files, inspect each named clip, and render the first and last frames before replacing a valued project. Hard-reload recovery of an unsaved environment was not tested.

The original edition’s 58-frame CLI-to-desktop-checkpoint agreement remains historical evidence for that artwork. It is separate from this edition’s 36-frame CLI verification; old desktop checkpoints and editor screenshots do not establish the revised artwork’s desktop status.

The visuals are substantially improved and ready for marketing review. Broad earth and water planes, repeated foliage vocabulary, and quieter overworld areas still leave room for art direction. Final art approval should come before any “AAA” positioning. The supplied videos are encoded artwork loops, not editor screen recordings.

sections.heading: Workflow accounting
paragraphs: The original four-agent workflow recorded 43,010,776 AI-agent tokens through October 27, 2026 at 17:57:51 UTC: 42,816,590 input and 194,186 output. The input total already includes 42,144,640 cached tokens; output already includes 48,653 reasoning tokens. Do not add these component counts again.

Those counters cover creative work, tests, retries, and revisions together. They exclude the original final response, subsequent packaging, the later art direction edition, and this guide’s publication work. They are agent-token accounting, not tokens consumed by PixelWall, an isolated art-generation cost, or a dollar estimate.

faqs.question: Do I need an AI agent or Pro to follow the guide?
faqs.answer: No agent is required to open and edit the supplied projects or run the saved CLI commands. Editing, Lua, native project files, and individual PNG exports are free. Creating GIFs, sprite sheets, atlases, or game packages requires Pro.

faqs.question: Can I edit the characters one layer at a time?
faqs.answer: Yes. Mira and the reedling each have three painted layers, with named Idle and Walk clips; Mira also has Jump. Open the native .pixelwall project to keep that structure. A flattened PNG does not preserve the editable layers.

faqs.question: Does the viewer demonstrate a complete PixelWall game engine?
faqs.answer: No. PixelWall creates and exports the artwork and animation frames. The separate viewer implements movement, jumping, camera follow, and parallax. It has no collision-aware gameplay or height-aware terrain.

faqs.question: Why does a saved export not fix the library-save failure?
faqs.answer: The local document library and exported project files are different storage paths. The library reached its budget in this test. A verified file checkpoint preserved the artwork, but the original library operation still failed.

title: Draw and save your first PixelWall sprite
description: Make your first pixel-art sprite in PixelWall. Learn the canvas, drawing tools, layers, PNG export, and editable project backups in five short steps.
intro: Start with a small canvas and a simple coin or heart. The current editor keeps multiple local documents, shows layers and a timeline, and lets you save native projects or individual raster frames for free.

steps.title: Create a small project
steps.text: Choose New project in the header. Enter a name, Width 16, Height 16, and a color mode. RGBA is a straightforward starting point. Confirm the new project.

steps.title: Place pixels
steps.text: Choose Pencil or press B, then choose a color in Colors and draw an outline. Eraser is E, Fill is F, and Sample color is I. Undo reverses a completed edit.

steps.title: Adjust the view
steps.text: Use the Zoom dropdown or Fit. Hand (H) pans the view. Zoom does not alter the saved pixel dimensions.

steps.title: Use layers
steps.text: Open Layers to add an image layer or group. Use the eye and lock controls to manage visibility and editing. Adjust opacity, blending, group membership, and cel X/Y offsets as needed.

steps.title: Keep both files
steps.text: Choose Save project backup in the header for a .pixelwall file. Export → Current frame PNG makes a finished raster image. Open project or image imports a saved native file or a supported image.

sections.heading: Save and recover
paragraphs: The document tabs keep separate projects on this device. Look for Saved on this device after a change. Recovery lists saved revisions; restoring one creates a new current revision while keeping recoverable history.
Local autosave is not cloud sync. If saving reports a storage or conflict error, keep the editor open and download a .pixelwall backup. Browser or operating-system cleanup can remove local storage.

sections.heading: What is free and how large can I work?
paragraphs: Drawing, animation editing, scripting and the command API are free. Editable PixelWall and supported sprite files, plus individual PNG, BMP and TGA frame exports, are free. Pro is $15 USD once for animated GIFs, sprite sheets and atlases, game package ZIPs, and saved export presets.

The document engine accepts canvas sides from 1 to 65,535 pixels, with at most 4,194,304 canvas pixels, up to 256 layers including groups, and up to 2048 frames. A document may store at most 16,777,216 image pixels across its distinct images. Linked cels share image data. Browser canvas limits and available memory can be lower, especially for very wide sprites. Check representative artwork on your device.

sections.heading: Keyboard and workspace preferences
paragraphs: Open Workspace settings to change tool shortcuts, sidebar position, and timeline height. Choose Floating to move the panel area, or dock it left or right. Pin panel keeps a section open while you switch tabs. Command/Ctrl+Z undoes, Command/Ctrl+S saves locally, and Command/Ctrl+K opens command search. Tool shortcuts apply when you are not typing in a field.

faqs.question: Which key selects Pencil?
faqs.answer: B in the current editor. The classic editor has its older controls and shortcuts.

faqs.question: Do I need Pro to save editable work?
faqs.answer: No. Native PixelWall and supported sprite exports are free, as are individual PNG, BMP, and TGA frames.

faqs.question: Where are my documents saved?
faqs.answer: In IndexedDB on this browser and device. Download a project backup to move or independently preserve your work.

title: Pixel art export formats
description: Choose editable projects, raster images, and animation exports. Understand generated files, browser download requests, and how to verify an automation handoff.
intro: Choose an editable project for future changes, a raster frame for a finished image, or a Pro batch format for an animation or game pipeline. Current-editor and classic package schemas differ; use the matching guide.

sections.heading: Current editor export choices
items: Editable PixelWall project · Free: a losslessly compressed .pixelwall file preserving the v4 document, including frames, layers, clips, palettes, linked images, tilesets, and metadata. Compact files require PixelWall 0.4.1 or later.
Editable sprite project · Free: a binary sprite file with supported layers, frames and metadata. Review import/export warnings and keep the .pixelwall source.
Current frame PNG, BMP, or TGA · Free: the active rendered frame at the selected scale. Native projects retain information that raster images flatten.
Animated GIF · Pro: the chosen clip and playback order with rounded GIF timing and limited color/transparency.
Sprite atlas PNG · Pro: an atlas PNG plus a separate JSON download describing rectangles, trimming offsets, source IDs, and durations. Allow multiple downloads.
Game package ZIP · Pro: atlas PNG and JSON, rendered frame PNGs, a native project, a manifest, and independent tileset/map data where present.
Saved export presets · Pro: keep reusable export options on this device with the Save export preset and Load saved preset controls.

sections.heading: Check that your download finished
paragraphs: “File generated” means PixelWall has created the file in the editor. The browser still needs to save it. A requested download can be blocked or require another click; the editor cannot observe whether the browser finished writing the file.

steps.title: Use the retained download link
steps.text: If no download appears, use DOWNLOAD FILE in the “Your download” panel. For an atlas, use both the PNG and JSON links and allow multiple downloads when your browser asks.

steps.title: Check the destination
steps.text: Wait for your browser’s download manager to finish, then locate the file in the folder your browser uses. Agents should verify the host’s download result or saved file rather than treating an export response as proof of a completed download.

steps.title: Open the result
steps.text: Open a PNG in an image viewer, reopen a .pixelwall backup in PixelWall, or load an atlas with its matching JSON. Keep the editor open until you have confirmed the files you need.

sections.heading: Retrieve exports through automation
paragraphs: In the current editor, window.pixelwall.export() requests browser downloads by default. Pass download:false to generate files without requesting a download. The returned result.exportResult separates the generated artifacts from browser download requests.

generated.status is generated when file creation has finished. Each entry in generated.files includes filename, mime, bytes, and a page-local object URL. generated.completedAt records generation time, not download completion. For a project export, bytes is the compressed file size.

download.status is requested when PixelWall attempted an automatic download click, or not_requested when it did not. Check download.files for each file’s request status, especially for an atlas’s PNG and JSON. These fields record the export’s automatic requests; they do not track later clicks on the retained download links. download.completion is unobservable and download.completedAt remains null.

Fetch the object URLs inside the same editor page. They expire after the next export, dismissal of the download panel, or editor unmount, including a reload or close. They are not public links or filesystem paths and cannot be fetched by a separate terminal process. Copy the bytes through your host’s file-transfer mechanism before they expire.

sections.heading: Choose rendered layers and references
paragraphs: For rendered formats, Layers selects Visible layers, Active layer, or Selected layers. Reference layers are omitted by default; enable Include reference layers to put them in the rendered output. Editor previews can still show visible references while you work.
Editable PixelWall and sprite saves retain the whole editable document, including reference layers. Scale, clip, and rendered-layer choices are not a way to flatten or reduce a native project save.

sections.heading: Atlas layout and metadata
paragraphs: Packed, horizontal, vertical, and grid layouts support padding, border extrusion, optional trimming, and optional power-of-two output dimensions. Packing does not rotate entries. The editor’s atlas limit is 8192 pixels per edge; an export fails if the chosen entries and spacing do not fit.

Trimmed frames record sourceSize and spriteSourceSize alongside their atlas frame rectangle. Durations are milliseconds. The JSON is an array of named frame entries, with clip/source information and slices in metadata. Preserve the JSON with the PNG.

Game ZIP uses sprites.png and sprites.json as a matched pair. For a separately downloaded atlas, verify that meta.image matches the PNG filename before loading JSON through an engine that follows that field. Scale changes rendered pixel dimensions; source document coordinates in clips and slices should be interpreted consistently in your own pipeline.

The current atlas metadata is not the classic pixelwall.sprite-atlas v2 schema. The frameTags field includes export-relative from/to ranges, explicit frameIndices, and source frame IDs. Non-contiguous selections use frameIndices; they are not the classic Phaser animation recipes.

sections.heading: Inside a current game package
items: manifest.json identifies the native project, atlas, rendered frames, tilesets, maps, clips, slices, and compatibility warnings.
sprites.png and sprites.json contain the selected frames in timeline order and their atlas metadata.
A named .pixelwall file preserves the editable source document.
frames/ contains individual rendered PNGs with source frame IDs and timing listed in the manifest.
tilesets/ contains independent tileset metadata and tile PNGs. Indexed documents with per-frame palette changes may emit separate palette variants.
maps/ contains Tiled-compatible orthogonal .tmj maps for frames with tilemap data, grouped by tile dimensions. No map files are invented for a document with no tilemaps.

sections.heading: GIF color and timing
paragraphs: The current encoder preserves up to 255 distinct opaque colors per frame plus transparency. When a frame exceeds that palette, it maps colors to a 216-color RGB grid. Alpha below 128 is transparent; remaining pixels become opaque.

Frame delays round to 10 ms units with a 10 ms minimum; a viewer may display very short delays differently. The current editor checks a 67,108,864-pixel budget over the entire scaled playback sequence. PNG and native project saves preserve original color information more faithfully.

sections.heading: Import and interoperability limits
paragraphs: PixelWall imports its native files, supported editable sprite files, PNG/BMP/TGA images, GIF animations, image sequences, and sprite sheets. A flattened format does not recover original layers. Animated PNG is rejected; use PNG frames or GIF. PNG 16-bit channels are reduced to 8 bits for editing.

PixelWall uses embedded ICC profiles for previews and image export, and converts PNG profile/gamma information when importing. Use Colors → Color profile to assign a profile or convert colors. Unsupported file features produce compatibility notes or a rejected import.

sections.heading: Classic packages and existing examples
paragraphs: The Phaser and PixiJS sample guides describe the classic editor’s established sprite package schema. Follow those guides using /editor/classic, or adapt your loader to the current atlas JSON. Existing downloadable example packages are labeled by their own contents.

faqs.question: Are editable sprite exports free?
faqs.answer: Yes, for the features the current encoder supports. Keep the native PixelWall project and review any compatibility notes.

faqs.question: Is a sprite atlas a regular spritesheet grid?
faqs.answer: It can be. Choose horizontal, vertical, or grid for regular layouts. Packed or trimmed layouts need their JSON rectangles and offsets.

faqs.question: Do game maps include collision shapes?
faqs.answer: No. Add game-specific collision or object data in the destination tool. PixelWall retains slices as source metadata; it does not automatically convert them to collision objects.

faqs.question: Can I retrieve an export after my automation call times out?
faqs.answer: In the same open editor, call window.pixelwall.exportResult() to read the latest retained handoff. It returns null before any export or after dismissal. Check its ID and filenames to identify the export; do not assume it belongs to the timed-out call. The handoff is kept only in memory and does not survive a reload.

sections.heading: Export and open the right files

steps.title: Create actual tilemap data
steps.text: In Tiles, create or choose an independent tileset, add a tilemap layer, and paint cells. Raster drawings alone do not create editable map cells.

steps.title: Download the game package
steps.text: Open Export and choose Game package ZIP. This requires Pro. The selected clip controls sprite atlas/rendered entries; the package preserves the full native project and exports its existing tilemap frames.

steps.title: Read the manifest
steps.text: Extract the ZIP. manifest.json lists every maps/ .tmj file and its source frame, timing, and tile dimensions.

steps.title: Open a .tmj map
steps.text: Open the map listed for your frame in Tiled. Keep maps/, tilesets/, and their relative structure intact. Tile images and .tsj definitions are external files in the package.

steps.title: Retain the source project
steps.text: Keep the included .pixelwall file as your editable PixelWall source. Tiled map round-trip import is not currently available.

sections.heading: Map structure and preserved data
paragraphs: Maps are finite and orthogonal. Tilemap layers sharing tile dimensions are grouped per frame. Different tile sizes produce separate maps. Image-collection .tsj tilesets reference individual PNG tiles.

Cell flags preserve supported flips and quarter-turn rotations. Layer visibility, opacity, offsets, locking, source IDs, and parent metadata are carried where supported. Layer groups are represented through flattened map layers and source properties; the native project keeps the original structure.

Indexed projects can emit multiple tileset palette variants. Maps reference the palette variant for their source frame. Numeric global tile IDs are package-local; use the manifest and PixelWall source IDs when correlating exports.

sections.heading: Read compatibility warnings
paragraphs: manifest.json lists limitations such as a layer blend mode that Tiled does not support. The original setting remains in properties and the native project. Rendered frame PNGs show the composite artwork, including raster layers that are not separate Tiled tile layers.

The package does not generate collision objects or animated-tile definitions. It exports per-frame map snapshots; game-specific runtime animation is your pipeline’s responsibility. External tileset sources must be available as embedded pixel data before game-package export.
JSON format declarations describe the emitted schema. They are not evidence that every version of Tiled or every game-engine loader has been tested.

sections.heading: Your analytics choices
paragraphs: On pixelwall.dev, public pages and both web editors share Privacy preferences. Essential only is the default: it sends only anonymous totals for page visits, first meaningful edits, automation actions and outcomes (including previews, validation and file retrieval), recognized public navigation, downloads, manual or automated export outcomes and checkout starts, with no persistent visitor ID or analytics cookie. Optional analytics stay off until you choose Usage analytics or Enhanced diagnostics. Do Not Track and Global Privacy Control keep both analytics channels disabled. You can change your choice from Privacy preferences at any time.

Usage analytics shares page categories, recognized navigation and download clicks, feature use, automation edits and operation outcomes, storage and export results, whether an export was manual or automated, Pro interactions, and basic browser/device details with PostHog. Optional standard pageviews use a canonical page category address rather than a full visited URL; coarse referral categories describe the current page’s immediate source. Optional analytics use a stored browser identifier to recognize repeat visits.

Enhanced diagnostics adds performance measurements and scrubbed error reports. No privacy level records sessions, replays, or automatically captures page text and clicks. Artwork, imported files, document and layer names, license and purchase identifiers, scripts, error messages, and full URLs are excluded from analytics.

Optional activity before permission is discarded rather than collected later. Earlier Required only refusals continue to keep all analytics off until you save a new choice. Withdrawing optional permission stops optional collection immediately and synchronizes the preference across tabs. If a preference cannot be saved, all analytics stay disabled for that visit.

Desktop apps do not use site analytics. Packaged desktop versions that offer Help → Share anonymous MCP usage can send anonymous operation and outcome counts only after you enable that separate setting. It is off by default and independent from allowing a local agent connection. Reports exclude artwork, scripts, filenames, paths, agent names and persistent identifiers. Disabling stops reporting and cancels pending requests; offline activity is never queued or backfilled. Version 0.5.0 and earlier do not have this reporting control. The standalone browser bundle, CLI, local development and private previews remain untracked. Desktop update checks request release information separately.

paragraphs: Each of the three frames is 16 × 16 pixels with one artwork layer. The default clip uses 125 ms per frame and loops forward. The PNG sheet has three full-size cells in a horizontal row without padding.

The GIF uses PixelWall’s normal GIF encoder. Its frame times round to centiseconds, while the JSON keeps the original per-frame durations. The project file preserves editable data rather than flattening the image.

sections.heading: Reuse the artwork
paragraphs: You may use and modify this sample artwork in personal and commercial projects. Attribution to PixelWall is appreciated but not required. This permission covers the included example artwork, not the application source.

title: Draw and edit with scripts and commands
description: Run free Lua scripts or JSON command batches in PixelWall, and use the shared browser API or CLI. Edit images, colors, palettes and tiles, and build blocking dialogs with Lua.
intro: Choose Lua 5.4 or PixelWall commands in the Scripts panel for repeatable pixel work. The browser API and standalone CLI use the same editing engine. Scripting is free; Pro export formats keep their license requirements.

sections.heading: Run a command batch in the editor

steps.title: Open Scripts
steps.text: Choose the Scripts panel beside Layers, Colors, Effects, and Tiles.

steps.title: Start with the command reference
steps.text: Choose Command reference to inspect available command names and fields. Inspect document shows the active document summary and revision.

steps.title: Enter JSON
steps.text: Paste a JSON command or array into Command batch (JSON), then choose Run command batch. A successful batch is one undoable edit.

steps.title: Inspect and save
steps.text: Check the canvas and command result. Undo if needed, then save locally or download a native project backup.

sections.heading: Run a Lua script
paragraphs: Choose Lua 5.4 in the Scripts panel, enter or open a .lua file, and choose Run Lua script. Check the canvas and printed result; Undo restores the previous artwork. This example adds one colored pixel on a new layer.
sections.code:
app.transaction("Add a pixel", function()
  local layer = app.sprite:newLayer()
  layer.name = "Lua drawing"
  local image = Image(app.sprite.width, app.sprite.height)
  image:drawPixel(0, 0, Color{r=255, g=107, b=87})
  app.sprite:newCel(layer, app.frame, image, Point(0, 0))
end)
print("Pixel added")

sections.heading: What scripts can do
paragraphs: Commands cover document/layer/frame operations, cels, drawing, selections/transforms, palettes, effects, clips, 2D motion, particles, tilesets, and tilemap painting. Use the command reference shipped with your build for the exact fields and supported options.

Lua Palette objects follow the effective per-frame palette keys. Scripts can edit those keys, generate a palette with app.command.ColorQuantization, and convert RGBA, indexed, or grayscale artwork with app.command.ChangePixelFormat. These operations preserve shared image links where possible and participate in transaction rollback.

The browser interface exposes window.pixelwall for structured operations and previews. If the browser provides a compatible modelContext tool-registration surface, PixelWall registers the same ordinary tools there. Availability depends on the host browser; PixelWall itself contains no AI assistant or generator.

sections.heading: Runtime boundaries
paragraphs: The editor runs Lua 5.4 scripts and structured JSON commands. Lua supports Sprite, Image, Color, selections, palettes, tilesets, color profiles and transactions. Unsupported APIs report a compatibility error. Each successful run is one undoable edit, including its selection and foreground/background changes.

Lua dialogs can ask for text, numbers, colors and other supported inputs, then resume the same script. Cancel discards staged artwork. Time, memory and image-size limits apply; Lua has no arbitrary file, network or process access. The separate CLI JavaScript script command loads an explicitly chosen local module with ordinary Node.js access.

sections.heading: A realistic scene workflow
paragraphs: Follow the 600 × 350 woodland crossing tutorial for a complete shape-command scene, bounded Lua detail, progress polling, recovery after a caller timeout, explicit export results, and compact project backups.

sections.heading: Licensing is consistent
paragraphs: Drawing, animation editing, scripting and the command API are free. Editable PixelWall and supported sprite files, plus individual PNG, BMP and TGA frame exports, are free. Pro is $15 USD once for animated GIFs, sprite sheets and atlases, game package ZIPs, and saved export presets.
Calling a GIF, atlas, or ZIP export through an API or CLI does not bypass Pro verification. Editing a project with a script and saving that editable project remain free.

title: Use the PixelWall browser command API
description: Inspect revisions, apply undoable command batches, save locally, preview PNGs, and invoke the same licensed exports as the editor.
intro: A running current editor exposes version 1 of window.pixelwall. The API acts on the active document and uses the shared command engine. It is intended for tools you deliberately run or connect.

sections.heading: Apply a revision-checked edit
paragraphs: Wait until the workspace has opened a document. inspect() returns a document summary and its current revision. Pass expectedRevision to reject an edit if the document changed after inspection. Omit frameId and layerId to use the active targets, or supply explicit IDs from your own document workflow.

sections.heading: Available methods
items: version: current browser API version, presently 1.
inspect(): current document summary, revision, and latestOperation. commands(): command descriptions and field reference.

apply({commands, expectedRevision?, label?, wait?, requestKey?}): apply 1–2000 commands, limited to 16 MiB of JSON, as one undoable change. wait:false returns an operationId before processing; poll operation(id) for staged commandsProcessed, commandsTotal, revision, completion, or error. A requestKey makes an identical retry reuse the retained result in this editor session; a mismatched or expired key is rejected. The session retains up to 1,024 request keys and 64 operation results.
runLua({source, params?, timeoutMs?, expectedRevision?}): run a bounded Lua script with the current document, selection and colors; successful changes are one undoable transaction.
colorProfile(options): inspect, assign or convert a document color profile through the editor’s color manager.
newDocument(options): save the previous document and activate a new one.
preview({frameId?, scale?}): return an in-memory PNG preview at up to 8× scale.

capturePreview(): retain an immutable baseline for a later visual comparison. The preview and comparison helpers can target frames, layers, crops, and contact-sheet layouts where supported by the current editor.
validate({commands, expectedRevision?, timeoutMs?}): preflight a command batch without committing it. The timeout bounds validation work; it is not a runtime estimate for applying the batch.
cancel(operationId): request cancellation of a running batch. Cancellation is checked between commands, and completed commands remain staged until the transaction commits or rolls back.
save(): await a durable local save. It does not download a backup or create cloud storage.

export(options): generate files and request browser downloads by default; pass download:false to generate retrievable files without clicking. The returned exportResult separates generated.files from download status, including per-file requests. exportResult() retrieves the latest handoff. Object URLs live until the next export, dismissal, or editor unmount; browser completion is unobservable.
undo() and redo(): use the active document’s editing history.

sections.heading: Behavior and limits
paragraphs: An invalid command or mismatched expectedRevision rejects the batch. Catch errors and show them to the user; do not assume that an export or save completed because a call began. The UI’s memory, document, storage, and format limits still apply.

The API is local to the page. It is not an unauthenticated network editing server and does not upload projects. A user-connected external tool may call it, but PixelWall does not embed AI. The CLI and opt-in desktop MCP provide corresponding local workflows.

sections.heading: Long edits and file handoff
paragraphs: commandsProcessed counts staged commands. A completed operation has committed once; a failed operation leaves no partial edit. If a client stops waiting, inspect latestOperation before retrying. Save after completion to make the edit durable. The operation log is page-local and disappears on reload.

Use export({format:"project", download:false}) for a compact editable backup or format:"png" for a finished frame. Read each generated file URL inside the same page and confirm persistence in your host; a generated file is not proof of a completed download.

links.label: Follow the complete workflow and recovery example

title: Use the standalone PixelWall CLI
description: Create and edit native sprite documents, render individual frames, import supported formats, and run paid batch exports with a signed ownership license.
intro: The CLI uses the same document engine as the current editor and runs locally with Node.js 22.13 or newer. The downloadable bundle includes its JavaScript dependencies; it does not need an app server or embedded AI.

sections.heading: Download and start
paragraphs: Download and extract the CLI bundle. Open a terminal in the extracted folder and run node pixelwall.mjs help. The examples below use the bundled file directly; an installed pixelwall command accepts the same arguments.
sections.code:
node pixelwall.mjs help
node pixelwall.mjs new --width 32 --height 32 --name Hero --out hero.pixelwall
node pixelwall.mjs inspect hero.pixelwall
node pixelwall.mjs render hero.pixelwall --frame 0 --scale 4 --out hero.png

sections.heading: Apply command files or a trusted script
paragraphs: Put the JSON command array from the scripting guide into edits.json. apply reads it and writes the resulting native document. script loads the JavaScript module you explicitly choose; the module can access ordinary Node facilities.

sections.heading: Run a Lua script
paragraphs: Lua scripts run locally with supported sprite-editing APIs. Use --params for app.params and --out-dir when a script edits more than one project. The default time limit is 3 seconds; --timeout can raise it to 10000 milliseconds. The Lua worker cannot read arbitrary files or use the network.
sections.code:
node pixelwall.mjs script hero.pixelwall --script ./draw.lua --out hero-scripted.pixelwall
node pixelwall.mjs profile hero.pixelwall --convert sRGB --out hero-srgb.pixelwall

sections.heading: Import and export
items: import art.ase --out hero.pixelwall reads a supported binary sprite file. PNG, BMP, TGA, GIF, and native inputs are also supported.
import sheet.png --frame-width 32 --frame-height 32 --out hero.pixelwall slices a PNG sheet; margin, spacing, count, order, and duration options are available.
import-sequence frame1.png frame2.png --duration 100 --out hero.pixelwall combines PNG files in the supplied order.
export hero.pixelwall --format ase --out hero.ase writes a supported editable sprite document for free.
render writes a single PNG frame. export with png, bmp, or tga also writes a free individual frame.
export with gif, sheet, atlas, or zip requires a valid Pro ownership license. Use sheet for a fixed-column sheet and atlas for trimming and packing.
sections.code:
node pixelwall.mjs export hero.pixelwall --format atlas --trim --padding 2 --extrude 1 --power-of-two --out hero-atlas.png --license license.txt
node pixelwall.mjs export hero.pixelwall --format gif --clip Walk --out hero-walk.gif --license license.txt
node pixelwall.mjs export hero.pixelwall --format zip --out hero-game.zip --license license.txt

sections.heading: License and format caveats
paragraphs: Supply the downloaded ownership license with --license, or supply the raw PW2 code using PIXELWALL_PRO_LICENSE. A valid signed PW2 license verifies offline against the public keys included in the build. Existing PW1 codes need one online conversion first.

Frame selectors are zero-based indices or frame IDs. --clip accepts a clip ID or exact name. CLI scale supports integer factors from 1 to 64, subject to output memory limits; the interactive editor exposes 1×, 2×, 4×, and 8× choices.

The CLI runs Lua sprite-editing scripts in a bounded worker. File features outside the documented format support may not survive import and export. Read warnings on stderr and keep the source file. Individual PNG/BMP/TGA images cannot preserve editable layers or clips.

sections.heading: Compact native files and readable JSON
paragraphs: Current PixelWall writes losslessly compressed PWPZ .pixelwall files and reads both compact and legacy JSON projects. A .json output or export --format json keeps an inspectable JSON payload. Update older desktop or CLI installations before opening compact files.

title: Keep PixelWall, projects, and Pro available offline
description: Download the standalone browser app and CLI, run the editor over local HTTP, and keep a signed Pro license and independent project backups.
intro: Offline use requires the editor’s files, your artwork, and any Pro ownership license to be available on the device. Keep separate backups of all three. The current downloads can run without the hosted application server.

sections.heading: Download the app and CLI
paragraphs: The standalone app ZIP contains a browser editor bundle, run-local.mjs, and a README. Extract it, read the included instructions, and run node run-local.mjs from that folder. Open the localhost URL printed by the local server. Node.js 22.13 or newer is required for the included launcher.

Use the local HTTP launcher instead of double-clicking index.html. Browser module loading, IndexedDB, and service-worker behavior depend on a supported origin. Keep using the same local address and port to reopen the same browser document library.
The CLI ZIP is a separate local-file command-line tool. It uses the same document engine and supports free individual-frame/native exports and licensed batch formats.

links.label: Download the standalone PixelWall app ZIP

sections.heading: Install the browser app shell
paragraphs: A supported browser can install or cache the editor after it successfully loads the complete app shell. Open it once while connected, allow preparation to finish, and verify an offline reopen before depending on it. Installation prompts differ by browser.

A hosted shell can still be removed by browser or operating-system cleanup. The downloaded bundle is an independent copy; its local launcher does not need the PixelWall application server. Keep your project backups outside browser storage.

steps.title: Save the license after checkout
steps.text: Choose Pro in the hosted editor, complete the $15 one-time purchase, and download your private ownership license.

steps.title: Restore in the offline app
steps.text: Open Pro → Restore Pro and paste the complete PW2 code. A compatible build verifies it locally with no expiry.

steps.title: Convert an older recovery code
steps.text: A valid PW1 code must reach the configured storefront once to obtain a signed PW2 ownership license. Keep the old code until conversion succeeds.

steps.title: Back up the app and artwork
steps.text: The license restores export access only. Save your app ZIP, license file, and native .pixelwall documents separately.

sections.heading: Use the desktop app
paragraphs: Get the Mac, Windows, or Linux app from the Downloads page. It includes the same drawing and animation studio and works offline.

Version 0.3.2 adds in-app updates. Choose Check for Updates… from the PixelWall menu on Mac or Help on Windows and Linux, download the update, then choose Restart to update. PixelWall saves your artwork first; Later lets you keep editing. If you are using 0.3.1 or earlier, install the latest version once from the Downloads page to get this feature.
Your desktop projects stay on your device. To move artwork between the browser and desktop app, save and open .pixelwall project files, then restore Pro with your ownership license.

sections.heading: Storage and ownership limits
paragraphs: The browser library uses IndexedDB, incremental image records, and bounded recovery versions. The default library budget is 96 MiB with up to 40 recovery versions per document, retaining the latest required recovery versions. Browser quota may be lower. A save error requires attention and a downloaded backup before closing.

An active online refund or dispute check can update access on that device. A non-expiring license already held by a disconnected app cannot be instantly revoked remotely. Offline ownership does not promise indefinite operation of the hosted store.

title: Understand native file and color compatibility
description: Understand compact .pixelwall backups, legacy JSON support, version requirements, and readable JSON export, alongside editable sprite and color compatibility.
intro: PixelWall saves layered artwork in its native v4 format and a supported binary sprite format. Keep your original source and inspect compatibility notes when moving complex artwork between tools.

sections.heading: Compact projects and version compatibility
paragraphs: PixelWall 0.4.1 saves native .pixelwall backups in a losslessly compressed container identified by PWPZ. Compression changes how the project is stored, while keeping layers, frames, linked images, palettes, tilesets, and metadata editable. It does not flatten the artwork or reduce image quality.

The web editor, desktop app, and CLI read both compact files and supported legacy JSON projects. Older PixelWall versions cannot read the compact container. Update the receiving desktop app or CLI to 0.4.1 or later before sharing a new .pixelwall backup.

Compression savings depend on the artwork. Large flat-color areas and repeated data often compress well; a particular size reduction is not guaranteed. A smaller file also does not raise the editor’s document or memory limits.

links.label: Get the current desktop app or CLI
Keep local saves and independent backups

sections.heading: Export readable JSON for another tool
paragraphs: Use the current CLI’s export --format json command when a tool needs a readable project payload. This writes the document as plain JSON and leaves the compact source file unchanged. Renaming a .pixelwall file to .json does not decompress or convert it.

Run this command from the extracted CLI folder, using your own project and output paths. JSON export removes the compressed container; it does not downgrade the document schema or make newer features compatible with every older editor. Check that the receiving tool supports the document and inspect a reopened copy before relying on it.
sections.code:
node pixelwall.mjs export river.pixelwall --format json --out river.json
node pixelwall.mjs inspect river.json
