Download a compact river project to try
Verify a generated file and completed download

sections.heading: What editable files preserve
paragraphs: Native PixelWall documents retain layers and groups, frames and cels, linked image references, color mode and palettes, clips, slices, independent tilesets, tilemap data, and metadata. Linked cels reference shared image records.

Supported binary sprite structures include RGBA, grayscale and indexed cel data; layers and groups; linked cels; frame timing and tags; slices, pivots, and user metadata; and supported embedded tilemap/tileset data. Preservation of a record does not guarantee every external application interprets it identically.

Unsupported structures can be rejected or reported as compatibility notes. External tilesets need available pixel data for rendered/game-package output. Unchanged source metadata may be retained where supported, but arbitrary unknown features are not guaranteed to survive every edit.

For an external tileset, use Tiles → Choose source & embed to select the matching sprite source. The editor verifies its grid and color mode and embeds it as one undoable edit. It never follows external paths automatically.

sections.heading: Color mode and profile limits
paragraphs: PixelWall keeps pixel values in the document’s working profile, with sRGB as the default. Embedded ICC profiles drive color conversion for previews and exported images. Assign changes how values are interpreted; Convert changes values to preserve appearance. PNG import converts embedded ICC or gamma information to sRGB. The current profile engine supports RGB and gray profiles.

RGBA stores color and alpha. Grayscale stores equal RGB channels with alpha. Indexed mode keeps palette indices, per-frame palettes and the transparent index. Conversion preserves linked cels when their effective palettes agree and separates them when palette changes require different pixels.

PNG imports support common bit depths and interlacing. Sixteen-bit channels become eight-bit editing values. Animated PNG is rejected; import a PNG sequence or GIF instead. GIF import preserves rendered animation frames and timing rather than the source layer structure.

sections.heading: Raster and 3D boundaries
paragraphs: PNG, BMP, TGA and GIF are rendered images, so they flatten editable layers. Some BMP/TGA variants have limited alpha, palette, or compression support; read the actual import error or warning rather than assuming every historical variant is supported.

PixelWall’s text tool rasterizes a bitmap font or command-supplied bitmap glyphs; it is not a full typography engine. Its motion and particles produce editable 2D frames. 3D model import/rendering is deferred.

sections.heading: Scripting compatibility
paragraphs: Choose Lua 5.4 in the Scripts panel to edit and run scripts using supported sprite-editing APIs. Images support pixel and byte access, crop/copy, nearest resizing, flips and compositing. Colors support RGB, gray, indexed, HSV and HSL values. Palette objects follow per-frame palette keys; ColorQuantization can generate colors, and ChangePixelFormat converts RGBA, indexed, or grayscale artwork. Blocking dialogs retain script variables across user input. Each successful run is undoable; failed or cancelled scripts leave staged artwork unapplied. Time and memory limits and unsupported API errors are explicit. Extension packages can provide palettes and explicit Lua command sessions; persistent plug-ins and advanced widgets are not supported.

Scripts can create and edit tilesets, insert or delete tiles, and assign tilesets to tilemap layers. ColorSpace values can assign working profiles or convert sprite colors. Imported ICC profiles are available to the script; arbitrary file and network access are unavailable.

sections.heading: Capacity and practical checking
paragraphs: The document engine accepts canvas sides from 1 to 65,535 pixels, with at most 4,194,304 canvas pixels, up to 256 layers including groups, and up to 2048 frames. A document may store at most 16,777,216 image pixels across its distinct images. Linked cels share image data. Browser canvas limits and available memory can be lower, especially for very wide sprites. Check representative artwork on your device.

Large layers, long clips, many palette variants, and scaled exports can hit memory or format budgets before the document validation maximum. Check a representative import, edit, export, and reopen cycle for the features your project uses.

title: Use PixelWall with an AI coding agent
description: Connect a coding agent through PixelWall's local CLI, browser command API, local desktop MCP, Lua scripting, or deliberate browser and desktop control. Includes editable scene components and a complete animated sprite example.
intro: PixelWall does not contain an AI model. An external agent can create and revise artwork when its environment can run local commands, execute code in the editor page, or control the browser or desktop interface. The agent still uses PixelWall's normal editing, saving, and export rules.

sections.heading: Choose the interface your agent can reach
items: Code execution with Node.js 22.13 or newer: use the downloadable CLI for local project files, command batches, Lua scripts, rendered previews, and exports. This is the most direct option when the agent has a terminal but no interactive canvas.
Browser page execution: a running current editor exposes window.pixelwall version 1 for inspection, revision-checked command batches, Lua, previews, saves, exports, Undo, and Redo.
Browser or desktop computer control: an agent with approved mouse, keyboard, screen, and file access can operate the visible editor. The desktop Help menu links back to this guide.

Local desktop MCP: PixelWall 0.5.0 can expose the running desktop window through an opt-in authenticated local launcher. It requires Node.js 22.13 or newer, the downloaded CLI bundle, and a user-selected export folder; it does not provide cloud or remote access.
Compatible browser tool registration: when a host supplies a modelContext registration surface, the editor registers its ordinary command tools there. Availability comes from the host environment.
Read-only web or chat access: the agent can read these pages but cannot edit PixelWall unless its host also provides one of the interfaces above.

sections.heading: What is available today
paragraphs: The supported automation surfaces are the local CLI, window.pixelwall in the current editor, the opt-in local desktop MCP launcher, bounded Lua 5.4 scripts, JSON command batches, and deliberate computer control. They use the same document and rendering engine in the web and desktop editors.

PixelWall does not publish a hosted MCP service, public REST editing API, JavaScript or Python SDK, or universal agent protocol. There is no automatic connection from an arbitrary chat. An agent needs explicit access to the local CLI, the running editor page, the opted-in desktop launcher, or the visible application.

links.label: Connect the local desktop MCP launcher

sections.heading: Run the complete ninja-panda example
paragraphs: This example uses 63 ordinary PixelWall commands to create a 24 × 24 ninja panda with nunchucks and three idle-animation frames. The downloadable command file is readable JSON. The finished project and first rendered frame let an agent compare its result before revising the commands.

Download and extract the CLI, then keep the command file in the same working folder. The first command creates an empty project. The second applies the complete animation as one edit. The third renders frame zero at 8× for inspection. Change the JSON and apply it to a fresh project for another revision.
sections.code:
node pixelwall.mjs new --width 24 --height 24 --name "Ninja Panda Idle" --out ninja-panda.pixelwall
node pixelwall.mjs apply ninja-panda.pixelwall --commands agent-ninja-panda-commands.json --out ninja-panda-animated.pixelwall
node pixelwall.mjs inspect ninja-panda-animated.pixelwall
node pixelwall.mjs render ninja-panda-animated.pixelwall --frame 0 --scale 8 --out ninja-panda-preview.png

sections.heading: A realistic scene workflow
paragraphs: Follow the 600 × 350 woodland crossing tutorial for a complete shape-command scene, bounded Lua detail, progress polling, recovery after a caller timeout, explicit export results, and compact project backups.

links.label: Build a woodland river crossing with shapes and bounded Lua

sections.heading: Safety, saving, and licensing
paragraphs: Inspect the current document and use expectedRevision before a browser edit when another person or tool may also change it. Treat a successful apply and a successful save as separate results. Keep a downloaded project backup before unattended batches or application replacement.

Scripts and commands cannot bypass format or Pro checks. Individual PNG, BMP, and TGA frames and editable projects are free. GIF, atlas, sheet, and game-package exports require a valid Pro license. Lua is bounded and has no arbitrary file, network, or process access; a deliberately selected CLI JavaScript module runs with ordinary Node.js access.

faqs.question: Can any ChatGPT conversation directly run PixelWall?
faqs.answer: No. The conversation's host must provide terminal access, browser page execution, or approved computer control and expose PixelWall through that environment.

faqs.question: Does PixelWall have an MCP server or public REST API?
faqs.answer: PixelWall supports an opt-in local desktop MCP launcher for a running desktop window. It requires the downloaded CLI and Node.js 22.13 or newer, uses authenticated local transport, and has no cloud or remote endpoint. Use the CLI, browser command API, Lua scripting, JSON command batches, or computer control when those are a better fit.

faqs.question: Can an agent create pixels without moving the mouse?
faqs.answer: Yes. A code-execution agent can build and revise native projects through the CLI, render PNG previews for inspection, and export supported formats.

title: Generate animated pixel water for an isometric scene
description: Use PixelWall's deterministic scene.water command to make a small animated pond, river, stream, waterfall, or shoreline, then refine it as ordinary editable frames.
intro: PixelWall can generate original 2D pixel water as an editable frame sequence. Choose a water form, top-down or isometric view, a seed, a season, and a compact palette; the result stays inside the same document and command workflow used by the editor, browser API, and CLI.

sections.heading: What this can do
paragraphs: In either the web editor or desktop app, choose Water scene. Pick a preset and view, adjust shoreline and water seeds separately, and watch the live preview. Use 3× repeat to inspect edge continuity. Generate water scene saves your current project first, then opens the result in a new project tab with separate Banks, Water, Rocks, and Grass & Reeds layers.

The scene.water command replaces the active document's blank artwork while preserving its document ID and canvas dimensions. It creates 12 frames by default, with 125 ms timing, and gives each frame a deterministic result for the same inputs. waterSeed varies the animation independently from the shoreline seed, rippleDensity controls highlight activity, and phaseOffset shifts the loop phase for an isolated piece. Set details to 0 for a quieter base pass, then paint highlights, banks, rocks, foam, or props on top.

Isometric view projects the ground, water, banks, and props into a 2:1 diamond scene with a visible soil edge. The result is ordinary editable 2D pixels; it does not create a heightfield, camera, lighting model, walkable terrain, or exported isometric tilemap.

media.alt: Animated isometric pixel stream with blue water, banks, rocks, and reeds.
media.caption: Original 96 × 80 looping stream animation generated from the documented command inputs.

sections.heading: Run a water pass in the browser

steps.title: Make a blank canvas
steps.text: Create a document at the size you want to keep. scene.water replaces the blank artwork but retains the document ID and dimensions, so choose the final canvas before running the command.

steps.title: Inspect and apply
steps.text: Read the current revision, then apply one scene.water command. Keep expectedRevision when another person or tool could edit the document at the same time.

steps.title: Tune the scene
steps.text: Choose scene pond, river, stream, waterfall, or shoreline; view top-down or isometric; seed; season spring, summer, autumn, or winter; and an optional palette object containing named role overrides. Width and height are 8–256 pixels, frames 1–32, durationMs 1–65535, details 0–4, rippleDensity 0–1, and phaseOffset an integer from −65535 to 65535.

steps.title: Refine and save
steps.text: Inspect the generated frames, add hand-painted details or a separate tile layer, preview the loop, and save. Render individual PNG frames freely; GIF, atlas, sheet, and game-package exports still follow the normal Pro license rules.

sections.heading: Run the same pass with the CLI
paragraphs: The CLI consumes the same JSON command batch as the browser command API. Start from a document with the final dimensions, apply the batch, inspect the resulting frame count and timing, and render a frame for review.
sections.code:
node pixelwall.mjs new --width 96 --height 80 --name "Isometric Stream" --out water.pixelwall
node pixelwall.mjs apply water.pixelwall --commands isometric-water.json --out water-generated.pixelwall
node pixelwall.mjs inspect water-generated.pixelwall
node pixelwall.mjs render water-generated.pixelwall --frame 0 --scale 6 --out water-preview.png

links.label: Download the isometric water command batch
Play the generated looping water preview

items: scene accepts pond, river, stream, waterfall, or shoreline.
view accepts top-down or isometric. Isometric is a 2D pixel treatment, not a 3D export.

season accepts spring, summer, autumn, or winter. Winter adds frozen pond edges. seed makes the shoreline variation repeatable; waterSeed independently makes the animated ripples repeatable. rippleDensity accepts 0–1 and phaseOffset shifts the loop phase.

frames defaults to 12 and durationMs to 125; details accepts 0–4 scene detail levels. Palette overrides must be an object of known role names such as water, foam, bank, ice, or rock with valid six- or eight-digit hex colors.

sections.heading: Build an isometric foundation
paragraphs: Use Isometric guide and Iso snap to align banks, bridges, rocks, and props. Set Iso tile width, then open Isometric shapes to stamp editable ground diamonds, raised blocks, or ramps. Water generation creates a separate project; it does not regenerate a single water layer inside existing hand-built artwork.

Isometric support is useful for composition and pixel alignment today. Generated scenes are marked spatiallyTileable:false; matching animation seeds do not guarantee seamless edges between separate pieces. PixelWall does not yet provide a full isometric map editor, height-aware terrain, depth sorting, or an isometric tilemap export format; assemble those systems in your game or tilemap tool after exporting the ordinary frames.

links.label: Use tilesets and tilemaps around the water

faqs.question: Does the generator copy or animate an existing water sprite?
faqs.answer: No. It creates original 2D pixel patterns from the command parameters and seed. You can still import or paint your own references and use the generated loop as a starting point.

faqs.question: Can I use it for a complete isometric game map?
faqs.answer: It can provide an animated water element and a useful isometric composition guide. It does not create terrain height, collision, depth sorting, or a complete isometric tilemap.

faqs.question: Will the same command produce the same water later?
faqs.answer: Yes, when the document dimensions and command inputs, including seed, are the same. Keep the JSON batch with the project so another agent can reproduce and revise the pass.

title: Build an isometric pixel-art foundation
description: Use PixelWall's 2:1 guide, snapping, editable diamond shapes, ramps, blocks, and deterministic water to prototype an isometric pixel-art scene.
intro: PixelWall's isometric toolkit is a 2D composition system: align pixels to a 2:1 diamond grid, stamp reusable terrain and building shapes, and combine those shapes with animated water. The same operations are available interactively and through command batches for agents.

steps.title: Choose a tile width
steps.text: Open the current editor and set Iso tile width to an even value such as 16 or 32. The width controls the horizontal span of the 2:1 diamond guide.

steps.title: Turn on alignment
steps.text: Enable Isometric guide to show the diamond grid, then enable Iso snap so drawing points land on the guide. Grid and snapping are editor aids; they do not alter the document's pixel dimensions.

steps.title: Stamp a starter tile
steps.text: Open Isometric shapes, choose Tile, Block, or Ramp, and use Stamp shape to place editable pixels on the current layer and frame. Move and refine them like any other PixelWall artwork.

media.alt: A pixel-art isometric composition with a diamond tile, raised block, and ramp in warm colors.
media.caption: Original isometric shape preview generated from draw.isometric commands.

sections.heading: Compose terrain and structures
paragraphs: The draw.isometric command creates one reusable 2D shape at a ground vertex. Choose shape tile, block, or ramp; set x and y, a width in multiples of four, elevation, and filled or outline treatment. Use leftColor and rightColor when you want a simple shaded face pair. The command is deterministic and remains ordinary editable pixels.

Use a small number of shared widths and elevations to keep an isometric scene readable. Place water, banks, paths, buildings, and props on layers that can be edited independently. A shape command does not infer neighboring terrain or collision.

sections.heading: Add water and export the foundation
paragraphs: Run scene.water on a blank document or with replace:true when you intentionally replace existing artwork. Use waterSeed to vary the animation independently from the shoreline geometry, rippleDensity for quieter or busier highlights, and phaseOffset when matching a water piece to a neighboring loop. The generator does not guarantee spatial tiling between separate documents or pieces.

PixelWall exports ordinary pixel frames and editable projects. It does not currently export a 3D scene, height-aware terrain, depth sorting, collision map, connected autotiles, or a universal isometric tilemap. Bring the rendered frames and your shape metadata into the game or map tool that owns those systems; those are the natural next pieces for a fuller isometric workflow.
sections.code:
node pixelwall.mjs new --width 96 --height 64 --name "Isometric Dock" --out dock.pixelwall
node pixelwall.mjs apply dock.pixelwall --commands isometric-dock.json --out dock-generated.pixelwall
node pixelwall.mjs render dock-generated.pixelwall --frame 0 --scale 4 --out dock-preview.png

links.label: Download the isometric shape command batch

faqs.question: Does isometric mode make a 3D model?
faqs.answer: No. It provides a 2:1 pixel grid, snapping, editable shape stamps, and 2D water treatments. Camera, height, lighting, collision, and depth systems remain outside PixelWall.

faqs.question: Can an agent reproduce the same scene?
faqs.answer: Yes. Keep the JSON command batch, document dimensions, shape parameters, and water seeds together. Repeating the same inputs produces the same generated pixels.

faqs.question: Can separate water pieces tile perfectly?
faqs.answer: No guarantee is provided for spatial tiling between separate generated pieces. Use one larger water document or hand-edit seams after rendering.

title: Build a woodland river crossing with shapes and bounded Lua
description: A practical 600 × 350 agent workflow with 576 commands, four editable layers, small Lua details, progress polling, explicit export handoff, and compact project backups.
intro: Use broad shapes for a scene, small pixel loops for details, and explicit checkpoints between batches. This reproducible woodland crossing keeps the artwork layered and editable in the web editor, desktop app, and CLI.

sections.heading: Start with shapes for broad areas
paragraphs: A 600 × 350 canvas contains 210,000 pixels per full-size layer. Filling it one pixel at a time through a scripting API adds unnecessary calls. Use draw.rect, draw.polygon, draw.ellipse, and draw.line for large areas and repeated marks. For a procedural raster, consider one cel.set pixel buffer within the command size limit.

This tutorial creates 576 commands across four full-size raster layers: Meadow and riverbed; River and bank details; Woodland footbridge; and Woodland and flowers. Broad shapes establish the meadow and irregular banks, shaded water carries the river, framed trees leave quiet areas around a simple wooden bridge, and small accents finish the crossing. The provided project and PNG let you inspect the result before running anything.

media.alt: A quiet blue pixel-art river winds through a woodland meadow beneath a small wooden footbridge, framed by trees, grasses, and flowers.
media.caption: A 600 × 350 woodland crossing built with 576 commands across four named editable raster layers.

links.label: Download the compact editable river project

sections.heading: Run the scene in the editor
paragraphs: Create a new 600 × 350 document first. The example uses the default layer-1 and frame-1 IDs and adds its own named layers, so apply it once to that new document. In Scripts → Commands, paste the downloaded JSON. A browser agent with page execution can use the following equivalent calls.

For a long operation, retain its operationId and poll in separate short calls. commandsProcessed counts staged commands; it does not mean they have committed. Only status completed confirms that the entire batch committed as one undoable edit.

sections.heading: Use Lua for a small, bounded detail
paragraphs: The companion script creates a detached 16 × 16 image, draws a few reed stems, and attaches it as a new cel on a named layer. The four 600 × 350 raster layers total 840,000 pixels, which stays within the Lua input budget while leaving room for this bounded 16 × 16 detail. Use small per-pixel loops for custom details; use shapes or bulk image data for large uniform areas. Detached images also let you assemble a detail before attaching it.

The Lua timeout can be raised to 10,000 ms, but larger limits do not turn an inefficient full-canvas loop into a good workflow. A timed-out or failed script discards its staged result. Inspect the revision after a failure and change the approach before retrying. Successful separate batches remain committed; rollback applies to the failed transaction.
sections.code:
-- Run after agent-river-commands.json on the 600 x 350 tutorial project.
-- Keep per-pixel work small: this detached 16 x 16 image has only 256 cells.
app.transaction("Add a small reed sprite", function()
  local image = Image(16, 16)
  local green = Color{r=137, g=181, b=89, a=255}
  for y = 2, 14 do
    image:drawPixel(7, y, green)
    if y > 6 then image:drawPixel(11, y, green) end
    if y > 9 then image:drawPixel(3, y, green) end
  end
  local layer = app.sprite:newLayer()
  layer.name = "Lua reed detail"
  app.sprite:newCel(layer, app.sprite.frames[1], image, Point(180, 180))
end)
print("Reed detail added as one undoable edit")

sections.heading: Recover when a caller stops waiting
paragraphs: A browser automation timeout may only mean the caller stopped waiting while the editor continued. Reconnect to the same open editor and inspect latestOperation, or look up the saved operationId with operation(id). Do not resend an edit solely because a client timed out.

If status is running, keep polling. If completed, inspect the new revision and save. If failed, read error and inspect the unchanged live document before correcting the batch. The operation log is in memory and retains the latest 64 operations; closing or reloading the editor removes it. After a reload, inspect artwork and saved recovery revisions before deciding whether to rerun anything.

Split very large jobs into at most 2,000 commands and 16 MiB of JSON per batch; use smaller batches when individual commands are expensive. Wait for completion, inspect the new revision, and save between batches. Each batch is one Undo step.

sections.heading: Separate file generation from download completion
paragraphs: Generate an export without clicking a download by passing download:false. The result separates generated files from download requests. Each file supplies its filename, MIME type, byte length, and a page-local object URL. A sheet export includes both PNG and JSON.

Read or copy the bytes in the same editor page before another export, dismissal, or editor close revokes those URLs. The URLs are not public network links and cannot be fetched from another process. For local automation without page execution, use the CLI to write to an explicit path.

download.status = requested means an anchor click was requested; browser download completion remains unobservable. Confirm the file in your own download manager or filesystem. exportResult() retrieves the latest handoff after a caller timeout.

sections.heading: Keep an editable backup and run the same workflow locally
paragraphs: Current PixelWall saves losslessly compressed PWPZ .pixelwall files and still opens legacy JSON project files. Layers, frames, image links, palettes, and project metadata stay editable. File size depends on the artwork; flat pixel scenes can compress especially well. Older PixelWall versions cannot read the new container, so update before opening it.

Use CLI --format json when you need a readable project payload for an older tool. Keep the compact project as your editable backup and use PNGs for finished transparent sprites. A local save and a downloaded backup are separate checkpoints.
sections.code:
node pixelwall.mjs new --width 600 --height 350 --name "Woodland crossing" --out river.pixelwall
node pixelwall.mjs apply river.pixelwall --commands agent-river-commands.json --out river.pixelwall
node pixelwall.mjs script river.pixelwall --script agent-river-detail.lua --timeout 10000 --out river-detailed.pixelwall
node pixelwall.mjs render river-detailed.pixelwall --frame 0 --out river.png
node pixelwall.mjs export river-detailed.pixelwall --format json --out river.json

title: Connect a local desktop MCP agent
description: Use PixelWall's opt-in authenticated local MCP launcher to inspect, edit, preview, export, and retrieve files from a running desktop window.
intro: PixelWall's desktop MCP connection is local and deliberate. It controls one open editor window through the same command API used by the desktop UI; it is not a hosted service or a remote editing endpoint.

sections.heading: Enable the connection
paragraphs: Install Node.js 22.13 or newer and download the PixelWall CLI bundle. In the desktop app, open Help, enable Allow local agent connection, and choose the export folder when prompted. PixelWall displays the launcher command; configure your MCP client to run it from the extracted CLI folder.

The launcher reads a short-lived authenticated session created by the desktop app and uses local stdio/loopback transport. One controller may use the open editor window at a time. Disable the Help-menu option, close the window, or stop the client to disconnect.
sections.code: node pixelwall-mcp.mjs

sections.heading: Use the editing and review tools
paragraphs: The launcher exposes inspection, project selection and import, command validation and application, operation polling and cancellation, previews, undo/redo, saving, exports, and export handoff results. Use wait:false for large batches, poll the returned operation, and include a requestKey when a caller may retry the same apply request.

capturePreview retains a session baseline for before/after review. Generated exports can be listed and read in bounded chunks, then saved through the approved folder. The browser still cannot report whether a later native download completed.

sections.heading: Optional anonymous MCP usage
paragraphs: New desktop builds offer Help → Share anonymous MCP usage, off by default. Enabling a local agent connection does not enable reporting. The separate choice shares only anonymous operation and outcome counts, including changed edits, previews, exports and verified artifact saves, with no artwork, scripts, paths or persistent identifiers.

Turn reporting off at any time from the same menu. Offline activity is not queued or backfilled. Desktop 0.5.0 and earlier cannot report MCP usage; the CLI and standalone browser bundle remain untracked.

sections.heading: Local safety limits
items: The connection has no cloud or remote access and cannot choose an arbitrary filesystem path. Artifact saving is confined to the folder selected in PixelWall.
Generated artifacts expire after 24 hours and are bounded to 64 files, 128 MiB total, and 64 MiB per file. Reads return at most 1 MiB per chunk and include checksum metadata.
Cancellation is checked between commands. It does not predict the runtime of an individual command, and validation timeout is a preflight bound rather than an apply runtime guarantee.

title: Generate editable scene components
description: Compose deterministic trees, rocks, river banks, bridges, and terrain accents with named editable layers and a shared palette.
intro: Scene components are small deterministic building blocks for agent-assisted pixel scenes. They produce ordinary named layers and shape commands, so you can inspect, revise, and paint over every result.

sections.heading: Compose a woodland crossing
paragraphs: Choose a kind such as tree, rock, bank, bridge, or terrain, then provide a seed, style, palette, position, and size. Repeat the same inputs for the same component. Keep a shared palette and place components on separate named layers so later edits remain local.

The polished 256 × 160 example combines a river base with clustered trees, faceted rocks, grassy banks, and a bridge that reaches both banks. It is a compact editable project rather than a flattened reference image.

sections.heading: Keep the workflow agent-friendly
paragraphs: Use broad component shapes for large areas and small detail commands for accents. Validate a batch before applying it, split long work into observable operations, and save after each completed stage. Scene components do not infer collision, height, depth sorting, autotiles, or a game map schema.

title: Review previews and generated files
description: Compare an editable document before and after an agent edit, then verify generated files through bounded local handoff metadata.
intro: PixelWall separates artwork review from file delivery. Capture a baseline before an edit, inspect the resulting preview and revision, then verify generated bytes and checksums through the current page or local desktop MCP connection.

sections.heading: Review an edit
paragraphs: Call capturePreview before applying a change when you need a stable comparison. After the operation completes, render the selected frame or comparison and check the revision, changed pixels, frame IDs, layer IDs, crop, and contact-sheet layout returned by the preview helper. A preview is evidence for review; it does not save the document.

sections.heading: Verify generated files
paragraphs: An export response means that file generation finished; it does not prove that a browser download completed. In the browser, fetch the page-local URL before the next export or editor unmount and verify the reported byte count. In desktop MCP, list artifacts, read at most 1 MiB at a time, verify the SHA-256 metadata, and save through the approved export folder.
Artifact records are temporary local handoff data. They expire after 24 hours and are bounded to 64 files, 128 MiB total, and 64 MiB per file.
